entities.summary:
The Kuomintang (KMT, Chinese Nationalist Party), founded by Sun Yat-sen in 1912 following the Xinhai Revolution that ended 2,000 years of imperial Chinese rule, was the ruling party of China from 1928 to 1949 under Chiang Kai-shek and has governed Taiwan since 1949. The KMT's history — encompassing the unification of China, defeat by the Chinese Communist Party, and the Republic of China on Taiwan — represents one of 20th-century history's most dramatic arcs of revolutionary rise and mainland defeat.

Sun Yat-sen founded the KMT from the Revolutionary Alliance to implement his Three Principles of the People: Nationalism, Democracy, and the People's Livelihood. After Sun's 1925 death, Chiang Kai-shek seized control and launched the Northern Expedition (1926-1928) unifying most of China against warlords. The 1927 Shanghai Massacre — Chiang's brutal suppression of Communist allies killing thousands — began the Chinese Civil War between KMT and CCP that would continue until 1949.

Chiang's government relocated to Taiwan after the Communist victory in 1949. Under KMT rule, Taiwan implemented land reform, industrialized rapidly, and transformed from a poor agricultural island to one of Asia's wealthiest economies (the 'Taiwan Miracle'). KMT rule became authoritarian under martial law (1949-1987), the world's longest-running martial law period. Taiwan's democratization in the 1990s ended KMT's single-party rule; the party now competes with the Democratic Progressive Party in Taiwan's vibrant democracy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Kuomintang's defeat in the Chinese Civil War and relocation to Taiwan created a political division whose resolution — reunification or independence — remains the most dangerous unresolved territorial dispute in the world.
